演奏馬辛可琴時，琴身垂直放置，琴腳靠於膝上。先以調音弦鈕將單弦調至配合歌手音域，: To play the masenqo the body is held upright with the spike resting on the knee. The single string is first tuned with the tuning peg to suit the singer's range, and the bow is then drawn across it; the bow may be in the left or the right hand, while the other hand lightly touches the upper part of the string, changing pitch by shifting its position. There is no fingerboard, so a beginner has to learn the stopping positions by ear and by muscle memory, and practise singing while playing.

馬辛可琴主要出現在厄立特里亞與衣索比亞傳統音樂中，阿茲瑪里在婚禮、宗教節慶與傳統: The masenqo appears mainly in the traditional music of Eritrea and Ethiopia, where the azmari accompanies singing with the bowed string at weddings, religious festivals and in traditional bars. From the middle of the twentieth century it also entered modern popular music and Ethiopian jazz: on the album Mulatu Plays Mulatu, Mulatu Astatke placed the masenqo and other traditional instruments such as the krar in Western jazz line-ups, and Girma Bèyènè brought it into contemporary jazz composition. Recordings can also be heard in the Éthiopiques series and at international festival performances.

Pitch is changed by the non-bowing hand touching the upper part of the string; there is no fingerboard, so intonation depends on the ear and on muscle memory. The tuning can be adjusted to the singer's range, and the instrument mainly accompanies azmari singing. Compared with the rebab it has only one string and is a spike fiddle, played with the spike against the knee and the body upright. The source does not describe how volume is controlled.

馬辛可琴流行於厄立特里亞與衣索比亞，常見於阿姆哈拉人、提格雷人與奧羅莫人社群。部: The masenqo is found in Eritrea and Ethiopia, commonly among the Amhara, Tigray and Oromo peoples. Some scholars think its origin may be connected with the rebab, which reached North Africa and the Middle East by Arab Islamic trade routes in the seventh and eighth centuries, though its form is different and it has only a single horsehair string. From the middle of the twentieth century it was played by the azmari at weddings, baptisms and in traditional bars, and it gradually joined modern popular music and Ethiopian jazz; Mulatu Astatke combined it with Western jazz line-ups, and UNESCO and the Ethiopian government have also promoted recordings for its preservation.
馬辛可琴（Masenqo）是厄立特里亞與衣索比亞的單弦弓弦樂器，屬弦鳴樂器中的單: The masenqo is a single-string bowed instrument of Eritrea and Ethiopia, a one-string spike fiddle among the chordophones, number 321.311. The soundbox is diamond-shaped or square, made of four boards glued together and covered with goatskin or rawhide; the neck passes through the body and projects below as a spike, and a horsehair string runs over the bridge to the tuning peg. It is played with the spike against the knee and the bow drawn across the string, while the other hand touches the upper part of the string to change the pitch. The azmari use it to accompany singing at weddings, religious festivals and in traditional bars.
